title: WHY DID GOD CREATE SEX TO FEEL GOOD?
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD CREATE SEX TO FEEL GOOD?
Does the Bible Ever Separate Pleasure From Holiness—or Have We Been Ashamed of Something God Himself Called Good?
There is a question many Christians have thought but were too embarrassed to say out loud.
If holiness matters so much to God…
why did He make sexual intimacy pleasurable?
Why design the human body with the capacity for extraordinary physical delight if pleasure itself is supposed to make us suspicious?
Some believers grew up hearing plenty about what sex could destroy, but almost nothing about why God created it.

And those warnings have biblical foundations. Sexual sin is real. Scripture never trivializes it. Paul commands believers to flee sexual immorality and glorify God with their bodies, and he explicitly connects sexual holiness with sanctification. See 1 Corinthians 6:18–20 and 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5.
But somewhere along the way, some Christians accidentally learned another lesson the Bible never actually teaches:
Sex must somehow become less holy the moment it feels intensely good.
And that is where we need to go back.
Before shame entered the human story.
Because if you want to understand what sex became, you first have to see what sex was before sin touched it.
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
Then comes the sentence that almost feels startling after generations of sexual shame:
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.”
The Hebrew behind “one flesh” is בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
Not two strangers borrowing each other’s bodies.
Not one person using another person as an instrument for gratification.
And Genesis places nakedness beside something equally important:
Before the serpent ever entered the garden, the human body was not embarrassing to God.
Marriage was not embarrassing to God.
Nakedness between husband and wife was not embarrassing to God.
Sexual union was not something humanity invented after the Fall.
God created their capacity for union.
And the Creator looked upon the world He had made and called His creation “very good.”
Maybe we have been asking, “How can something this pleasurable possibly be holy?”
when Scripture pushes us toward another question:
Why would holiness require God's good gifts to be joyless?
The Bible never establishes a universal equation that says pleasure equals righteousness. Plenty of sinful things can feel pleasurable for a moment.
But neither does Scripture establish the opposite equation:
Because sin did not invent pleasure.
Hunger is good; gluttony can corrupt it.
Money can accomplish good; greed can enslave a heart.
Authority can protect; power can become abusive.
Rest is good; laziness can distort it.
Sexual desire can belong within God's good creation; lust, exploitation, adultery, pornography, selfishness and sexual immorality can twist desire away from love, covenant and holiness.
The existence of a counterfeit does not prove the original was evil.
It proves something valuable was worth counterfeiting.
And then Scripture becomes even more uncomfortable for anyone trying to pretend biblical sexuality is merely reluctant reproduction.
Not an erotic novel from secular culture.
The father warns his son against adultery—and what is the alternative?
A marriage in which husband and wife tolerate intimacy solely to produce children?
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Then Scripture speaks openly of the husband's delight in his wife and tells him to remain captivated by her love.

The Hebrew imagery is remarkably strong. Proverbs 5:19 uses the verb רָוָה (ravah), carrying the sense of being filled, saturated, or drinking one's fill. The verse is not ashamed to describe marital attraction and satisfaction positively.
God could have inspired Solomon simply to say:
It does not merely tell the husband what forbidden bed to avoid.
It directs his affection back toward the woman with whom he has covenant.
That means biblical holiness is not merely the absence of forbidden desire.
The Bible does not simply say, “Don’t go there.”
And then there is Song of Songs.
A book Christians sometimes seem more embarrassed to read than God was to inspire.

The language is poetic rather than pornographic, covenantal rather than exploitative, but its celebration of embodied marital love is unmistakable. Song of Songs can speak of love as beautiful and delightful without treating those words as enemies of holiness.
God did not create marital intimacy and then apologize for making it pleasurable.
But there is another side of this truth that our culture desperately needs.
Because saying pleasure can be good is not the same thing as saying:
That is appetite enthroned as god.
And appetite makes a terrible god.
The biblical question is never simply:
“Can this desire be surrendered to Jesus Christ?”
“Ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body.”
Christian sexuality is not ultimately about how close you can walk to the edge without technically sinning.
It is about whether Jesus is Lord even here.
In the secret places nobody at church sees.
The Gospel does not declare your spirit God's property while leaving your sexuality outside the kingdom.
And this is precisely why sexual holiness is bigger than repression.
The New Testament language of sanctification—ἁγιασμός, hagiasmos—carries the idea of holiness, consecration, being set apart to God.
So biblical holiness does place boundaries around sexuality.
But those boundaries do not mean God hates sexuality.
You put fences around something precious.
And perhaps this is where someone reading this feels the article suddenly getting personal.
Because we are no longer discussing theology in the abstract.
but your sexual history still whispers another name over you.
Maybe nobody knows what you watch when you are alone.
Maybe you promised God you would stop.
Then walked into church on Sunday and lifted the same hands that were trembling with shame the night before.
Maybe somebody violated what God intended to be sacred.
And now even the word “sex” does not sound beautiful to you.
Maybe intimacy reminds you of betrayal.
Maybe somebody used Scripture to pressure you.
Maybe someone demanded your body and called that biblical marriage.
1 Corinthians 7 does not present marital intimacy as unilateral ownership.
“The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband: and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife.”
The Greek verb is ἐξουσιάζει — exousiazei, “has authority over.”
He applies the principle in both directions.

The passage therefore cannot honestly be reduced to “the husband gets whatever he demands.” Paul immediately speaks of mutuality and warns spouses against depriving one another except by mutual agreement for a limited spiritual purpose.
Biblical intimacy is not permission for coercion.
It is not permission for humiliation.
It is not permission for violence.
It is not permission to treat your spouse like property.
The New Testament takes two people and places both beneath Christ.
Because Christlike love does not ask merely:
And suddenly we discover why pleasure and holiness never needed to be enemies.
Holy marital intimacy is not merely pleasure received.
I am not shopping for another body.
I am not comparing you to pornography.
I am not performing for strangers.
That is radically different from the counterfeit our culture sells.
Your desire matters more than another person's dignity.
I will not separate your body from your person.
Desire will not become my master.
That last command reaches much deeper than sexual behavior.
Because Christianity is not fundamentally God giving sexually broken people a longer rulebook.
Christianity is Christ giving dead sinners life.
This is where the scandal becomes grace.
Because some of us desperately want an article about sex to end with rules.
Rules allow us to divide everybody into two camps.
People carrying secrets they have never spoken aloud.
And then Jesus walks straight through our categories.
Not pretending sexual sin does not matter.
But doing something infinitely more astonishing.
Remember the woman caught in adultery.
Jesus did not rename adultery righteousness.
But neither did He allow her sin to become the final sentence over her existence.
Grace did not say sin was harmless.
Grace made a new future possible.
Jesus does not save us because our sexual histories are spotless.
Jesus saves sinners because His blood is sufficient.
The cross is where every illusion dies.
The illusion that sexual freedom can save us.
The illusion that religious respectability can save us.
The illusion that virginity can save us.
The illusion that marriage can save us.
The illusion that being heterosexual can save us.
The illusion that avoiding one particular category of sexual sin can save us.
And when Christ saves, He does not merely forgive us so that we can continue bowing to the same masters.
Grace begins teaching us to walk differently.
This is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not God screaming, “You disgust Me.”
The Greek New Testament uses μετάνοια — metanoia — for repentance, language associated with a changed mind, a turning of orientation.
Jesus, my sexuality belongs to You too.
Even the parts of myself I am embarrassed to bring into prayer…
And maybe that is what somebody needs tonight.
Not another performance of religious perfection.
Come to Christ because you cannot clean yourself.
Your worst chapter is your name.
The cross was built for sinners who could not undo yesterday.
Sexual pleasure is therefore neither our savior nor our enemy.
It is a created capacity that must remain beneath the lordship of its Creator.

Within biblical marriage, Scripture can speak unapologetically of delight, satisfaction, mutuality and a marriage bed kept undefiled. Hebrews 13:4 holds those realities together: marriage is to be honored and the marriage bed kept pure, while sexual immorality and adultery remain subject to God's judgment.
That means the Bible does not force us to choose between pleasure and holiness.
It forces us to choose between worshiping pleasure and surrendering pleasure to God.
But God is not threatened by the goodness of what He created.
So if this exposed something hidden in you, don't hide behind religious language.
But sometimes bringing darkness into honest Christian community is one small way of saying:
If you know someone trapped in pornography, sexual shame, adultery, regret, loneliness or secret temptation, do not use this article as a weapon.
Because temptation has a strange way of making us forget truths we were certain about yesterday.
And not because anyone should be pressured into giving.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity.”
The Greek is particularly important here:
μὴ ἐξ ἀνάγκης — mē ex anankēs.
Christian generosity should come willingly from the heart.
So if you prayerfully choose to support Gospel Warrior, let it be worship expressed through willing generosity—not spiritual pressure.
And whether or not you are able to support financially, sharing matters.
Not to make yourself look religious.
Follow if you want to keep walking deeper into Scripture.
Because the deepest question was never merely:
“Why did God make sex feel good?”
“What happens when every pleasure, every desire, every wound, every failure and every hidden room of the human heart finally bows before Jesus Christ?”
When Christ becomes Lord of it.
Not when your past becomes imaginary.
When grace becomes greater than it.
Not when you finally become impressive enough for God.
When you discover that the crucified and risen Christ came for sinners who could never rewrite themselves.
You may have chapters you wish you could burn.
Jesus specializes in stories everybody else thought were already ruined.
And perhaps the sentence you need to carry with you after this article is this:
Your darkest sexual chapter does not have to become the final author of your story—the hands that were pierced for sinners are still rewriting lives.
